title: GXO and ASUS: separating robot plans from results
lead: Logistics company GXO plans to expand humanoid use after warehouse trials. ASUS is teaching a two-arm robot to pack computer accessories, but its stated speed and success rate remain targets.

news.title: Why NVIDIA's leadership change matters to robotics
news.summary: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. The change matters to an industry dependent on computing platforms, but does not establish that hardware production will stop.
news.details: On November 12, NVIDIA announced Jensen Huang's departure as president, chief executive and board member. Colette Kress became interim chief executive while retaining her chief financial officer duties; a permanent successor is still being sought. NVIDIA's filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission says the board accepted the resignation on November 11. That is the decision date, whereas November 12 is the public announcement date. The leadership change at a supplier of AI computing equipment is a confirmed event, rather than an inference from reports about the scandal.
news.technical_novelty: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. The change matters to an industry dependent on computing platforms, but does not establish that hardware production will stop. The crisis surrounding Huang has a separate investigative process: on November 10, independent directors said they had engaged outside lawyers to investigate. TechCrunch describes the controversy as arising from reported extramarital relationships and scrutiny of China-related chip sales. TechCrunch and Reuters independently reported the resignation, but reports of possible misconduct are not findings of that investigation. The cited official documents do not publish such findings. NVIDIA's board says operations, customer commitments and product plans should continue without interruption. That is the company's position about future operations; it does not independently establish that customers will see no disruption. Financial results and the accompanying investor call remain scheduled for November 17.
news.engineering_impact: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. The change matters to an industry dependent on computing platforms, but does not establish that hardware production will stop. The useful follow-up is whether concrete decisions support the promised continuity. NVIDIA kept its November 17 reporting date. Until further evidence appears, a change in executive leadership and a change in hardware capability remain different events, even when discussed in the same news cycle.
news.limitations: NVIDIA confirmed chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation and finance chief Colette Kress’s interim appointment. The change matters to an industry dependent on computing platforms, but does not establish that hardware production will stop. The useful follow-up is whether concrete decisions support the promised continuity. NVIDIA kept its November 17 reporting date. Until further evidence appears, a change in executive leadership and a change in hardware capability remain different events, even when discussed in the same news cycle.
news.evidence_status: Leadership change is confirmed by the official release and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing; an investigation and reported allegations are not findings of guilt.
news.body:
On November 12, NVIDIA announced Jensen Huang's departure as president, chief executive and board member. Colette Kress became interim chief executive while retaining her chief financial officer duties; a permanent successor is still being sought. NVIDIA's filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission says the board accepted the resignation on November 11. That is the decision date, whereas November 12 is the public announcement date. The leadership change at a supplier of AI computing equipment is a confirmed event, rather than an inference from reports about the scandal.

The crisis surrounding Huang has a separate investigative process: on November 10, independent directors said they had engaged outside lawyers to investigate. TechCrunch describes the controversy as arising from reported extramarital relationships and scrutiny of China-related chip sales. TechCrunch and Reuters independently reported the resignation, but reports of possible misconduct are not findings of that investigation. The cited official documents do not publish such findings. NVIDIA's board says operations, customer commitments and product plans should continue without interruption. That is the company's position about future operations; it does not independently establish that customers will see no disruption. Financial results and the accompanying investor call remain scheduled for November 17.

Robots need more than motors: their programs learn using computers and later run on selected hardware. Events at a major supplier therefore reach beyond its own offices. That connection does not justify inventing a particular consequence, however; the leadership statement does not announce the closure of a robotics program or the withdrawal of an engineering tool.

The useful follow-up is whether concrete decisions support the promised continuity. NVIDIA kept its November 17 reporting date. Until further evidence appears, a change in executive leadership and a change in hardware capability remain different events, even when discussed in the same news cycle.

news.title: ASUS teaches a robot to handle small bagged parts
news.summary: ASUS described a two-arm robot for packing motherboard accessories. At its own factory, it is testing learning from people's work, while high success remains a stated target.
news.details: On November 13, ASUS described Gallop, its robot program for factory workstations. Today it is a fixed-base, two-arm system learning to pack accessories for motherboards, the main circuit boards connecting a computer’s components, at an ASUS group plant. The station contains 15 small parts, many in thin transparent bags. ASUS sets a target of 99.5% success while completing a kit within 20 seconds. In the article, that is the required standard, not a published measurement of reliability already achieved. A wheeled version, customer pilots in 2027 and market availability in the second half of 2028 remain plans.
news.technical_novelty: ASUS described a two-arm robot for packing motherboard accessories. At its own factory, it is testing learning from people's work, while high success remains a stated target. ASUS describes four control layers: planning steps, separately checking their execution, reaching and grasping skills, and precise arm control. Fixed interfaces — agreed rules for exchanging data — connect them so that models can change without rebuilding the whole robot. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor computer runs the system. Training uses recordings of consenting workers, variations in computer-simulated conditions and demonstrations guided by a person wearing a headset and gloves. ASUS still plans to integrate its own touch-sensitive hand. The intended design should therefore not be mistaken for the exact configuration already operating on the current rig.
news.engineering_impact: ASUS described a two-arm robot for packing motherboard accessories. At its own factory, it is testing learning from people's work, while high success remains a stated target. The current fixed system and the planned wheeled robot also need separating. Moving between workstations and manipulating items at one table are different capabilities. ASUS describes development of the latter and plans to add the former, rather than demonstrating both together as a ready production offering.

The current fixed system and the planned wheeled robot also need separating. Moving between workstations and manipulating items at one table are different capabilities. ASUS describes development of the latter and plans to add the former, rather than demonstrating both together as a ready production offering.
news.evidence_status: Developer announcement; stated plans and capabilities are not an independent test.
news.body:
On November 13, ASUS described Gallop, its robot program for factory workstations. Today it is a fixed-base, two-arm system learning to pack accessories for motherboards, the main circuit boards connecting a computer’s components, at an ASUS group plant. The station contains 15 small parts, many in thin transparent bags. ASUS sets a target of 99.5% success while completing a kit within 20 seconds. In the article, that is the required standard, not a published measurement of reliability already achieved. A wheeled version, customer pilots in 2027 and market availability in the second half of 2028 remain plans.

ASUS describes four control layers: planning steps, separately checking their execution, reaching and grasping skills, and precise arm control. Fixed interfaces — agreed rules for exchanging data — connect them so that models can change without rebuilding the whole robot. An onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor computer runs the system. A thin bag is difficult to handle because contact can change its shape. A robot needs not only to move its hand but also to check that the item arrived where required. ASUS assigns step checking to a separate layer. Its detailed tests are not published, so no particular checking reliability can be attributed to that description.

The current fixed system and the planned wheeled robot also need separating. Moving between workstations and manipulating items at one table are different capabilities. ASUS describes development of the latter and plans to add the former, rather than demonstrating both together as a ready production offering.

news.title: A person's gaze helps identify which object to fetch
news.summary: A team including Tsinghua University recorded speech, gaze and robot actions to study household requests. The extra cue can clarify the intended object, while the integrated assistant still often fails to finish the job.
news.details: A team including Tsinghua University posted a research preprint on November 12 about grounding household robot requests in speech, measured gaze and video from the person's viewpoint. Its HEIR dataset pairs those signals with robot observations and recorded movements. An operator controlled the robot during data collection: these are demonstrations, not thousands of independently completed requests. Seventeen participants contributed 300 sessions totaling 38.56 hours. The evaluation covers identifying the intended object, planning steps, moving around and manipulating objects with the arms.
news.technical_novelty: A team including Tsinghua University recorded speech, gaze and robot actions to study household requests. The extra cue can clarify the intended object, while the integrated assistant still often fails to finish the job. The Tsinghua team’s system first interprets a request, then uses the current state to decide whether to continue a step, switch to the next one or finish. The authors compared models on recordings and ran separate autonomous experiments on a physical robot. The integrated system completed 18.52% of 27 evaluated requests. Better scores for individual actions do not establish equal reliability for the whole assistant. Gaze contributions were isolated mainly through controlled comparisons on recorded data; live sessions diverge in human behavior and object arrangement. The result does not establish dependable assistance in an arbitrary home or for a person outside the tested setting.
news.engineering_impact: A team including Tsinghua University recorded speech, gaze and robot actions to study household requests. The extra cue can clarify the intended object, while the integrated assistant still often fails to finish the job. The cue has a clear boundary: looking information does not replace locomotion or grasping. Errors accumulated between stages in the integrated test, so whole requests succeeded less often than individual actions. A useful source of data is therefore different from a ready independent household assistant.

The extra cue can clarify the intended object, while the integrated assistant still often fails to finish the job. The cue has a clear boundary: looking information does not replace locomotion or grasping. Errors accumulated between stages in the integrated test, so whole requests succeeded less often than individual actions. A useful source of data is therefore different from a ready independent household assistant.
news.evidence_status: Preprint and author-run experiments; independent reproduction is not confirmed.
news.organization: Tsinghua University; Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence; Fudan University; Yangu Robotics
news.body:
A team including Tsinghua University posted a research preprint on November 12 about grounding household robot requests in speech, measured gaze and video from the person's viewpoint. Its HEIR dataset pairs those signals with robot observations and recorded movements. An operator controlled the robot during data collection: these are demonstrations, not thousands of independently completed requests. Seventeen participants contributed 300 sessions totaling 38.56 hours. The evaluation covers identifying the intended object, planning steps, moving around and manipulating objects with the arms.

The Tsinghua team’s system first interprets a request, then uses the current state to decide whether to continue a step, switch to the next one or finish. The authors compared models on recordings and ran separate autonomous experiments on a physical robot. The integrated system completed 18.52% of 27 evaluated requests. Better scores for individual actions do not establish equal reliability for the whole assistant. Gaze contributions were isolated mainly through controlled comparisons on recorded data; live sessions diverge in human behavior and object arrangement. The result does not establish dependable assistance in an arbitrary home or for a person outside the tested setting.

When someone says to bring that thing, sound alone may not identify the chosen object. Gaze direction supplies another observable cue. This is not mind reading: researchers align measurements with images and words, then separately test whether the robot can travel, grasp the item and complete the request rather than merely name the right object.

The cue has a clear boundary: looking information does not replace locomotion or grasping. Errors accumulated between stages in the integrated test, so whole requests succeeded less often than individual actions. A useful source of data is therefore different from a ready independent household assistant.

news.title: Why a thousand-robot plan begins with conditions
news.summary: GXO and Apptronik want to expand warehouse humanoid trials. Up to 1,000 refers to a possible future scale after validation, not warehouses already filled with those robots.
news.details: Logistics company GXO and robot developer Apptronik announced a letter of intent on November 12 to expand warehouse trials of the human-shaped Apollo robot. Tests in live operations are planned from 2027, covering picking, case and tote movement, packing and sorting. The proposed scale is up to 1,000 robots over four years, explicitly conditional on meeting agreed productivity, safety and operational measures. Initial commercial deployment in North America is intended for late 2027. This is a conditional expansion plan, not an announcement that a thousand machines have been delivered.
news.technical_novelty: GXO and Apptronik want to expand warehouse humanoid trials. Up to 1,000 refers to a possible future scale after validation, not warehouses already filled with those robots. GXO and Apptronik envisage a service model: robot use would be provided as a service that can expand as applications become ready. Prices, maintenance coverage and the allocation of individual costs are not disclosed. GXO reports an earlier pilot for picking small consumer goods and evaluations of more than 50 logistics tasks at Apptronik's training facility. That facility is not fifty customer warehouses. Independent Forbes coverage highlights an economic limitation: GXO's chief executive had previously said humanoid investment had not yet paid off. The agreement itself provides no payback calculation for the future program.
news.engineering_impact: GXO and Apptronik want to expand warehouse humanoid trials. Up to 1,000 refers to a possible future scale after validation, not warehouses already filled with those robots. A service format describes how robots might be provided, not an automatic guarantee of value. Prices are not disclosed. The criteria allowing expansion are therefore more informative than the headline ceiling: they will distinguish a possible thousand machines from the smaller number that may prove useful on suitable jobs.
news.limitations: GXO and Apptronik want to expand warehouse humanoid trials. Up to 1,000 refers to a possible future scale after validation, not warehouses already filled with those robots. A service format describes how robots might be provided, not an automatic guarantee of value. Prices are not disclosed. The criteria allowing expansion are therefore more informative than the headline ceiling: they will distinguish a possible thousand machines from the smaller number that may prove useful on suitable jobs.
news.evidence_status: Developer announcement; stated plans and capabilities are not an independent test.
news.body:
Logistics company GXO and robot developer Apptronik announced a letter of intent on November 12 to expand warehouse trials of the human-shaped Apollo robot. Tests in live operations are planned from 2027, covering picking, case and tote movement, packing and sorting. The proposed scale is up to 1,000 robots over four years, explicitly conditional on meeting agreed productivity, safety and operational measures. Initial commercial deployment in North America is intended for late 2027. This is a conditional expansion plan, not an announcement that a thousand machines have been delivered.

GXO and Apptronik envisage a service model: robot use would be provided as a service that can expand as applications become ready. Prices, maintenance coverage and the allocation of individual costs are not disclosed. GXO reports an earlier pilot for picking small consumer goods and evaluations of more than 50 logistics tasks at Apptronik's training facility. That facility is not fifty customer warehouses. Independent Forbes coverage highlights an economic limitation: GXO's chief executive had previously said humanoid investment had not yet paid off. The agreement itself provides no payback calculation for the future program.

The shift is from asking whether a machine can lift an object to asking whether it can fit into warehouse work. Picking, transport and packing connect with people and existing equipment. One device succeeding in an empty test area does not show how many should be added to an operating shift or which tasks justify them.

A service format describes how robots might be provided, not an automatic guarantee of value. Prices are not disclosed. The criteria allowing expansion are therefore more informative than the headline ceiling: they will distinguish a possible thousand machines from the smaller number that may prove useful on suitable jobs.

news.title: Japanese driving software is being adapted for a Munich bus
news.summary: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich will apply experience with the Autoware automated-driving software to a full-size city bus. Controlled testing comes first, followed by planned route operation with safety personnel aboard.
news.details: Japan's TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich announced support on November 11 for automated-driving development on a full-size city bus in Munich. The basis is Autoware, automated-driving software whose development TIER IV leads. Its source code is available for study and modification. The bus still needs adaptation to local roads and testing. Bus manufacturer MAN is responsible for vehicle-control mechanisms and low-level software; the university handles sensor configuration and the driving system. After tests in controlled conditions, the partners plan operation on existing routes with personnel aboard to ensure safety.
news.technical_novelty: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich will apply experience with the Autoware automated-driving software to a full-size city bus. Controlled testing comes first, followed by planned route operation with safety personnel aboard. The effort uses a joint research center established in October. It draws on experience deploying the Autoware automated-driving software in Japanese buses, but does not simply install unchanged software on another vehicle: both the vehicle platform and road conditions differ. A university professor describes federal support of 20 million euros over three years for the Munich bus-development project. That is project-wide funding, not an announced budget solely for Autoware software. The release supplies no Munich route-trial results, measured reduction in crashes or promise to remove the onboard safety personnel at the outset.
news.engineering_impact: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich will apply experience with the Autoware automated-driving software to a full-size city bus. Controlled testing comes first, followed by planned route operation with safety personnel aboard. Passenger-route work is a planned stage in the announcement, not a published result. An onboard safety worker is part of that plan too. Automated does not mean people can already stop monitoring the journey, or that the road evaluation has been completed and the bus is ready for unrestricted service.
news.limitations: TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich will apply experience with the Autoware automated-driving software to a full-size city bus. Controlled testing comes first, followed by planned route operation with safety personnel aboard. Passenger-route work is a planned stage in the announcement, not a published result. An onboard safety worker is part of that plan too. Automated does not mean people can already stop monitoring the journey, or that the road evaluation has been completed and the bus is ready for unrestricted service.

news.organization: TIER IV; Technical University of Munich; MAN
news.body:
Japan's TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich announced support on November 11 for automated-driving development on a full-size city bus in Munich. The basis is Autoware, automated-driving software whose development TIER IV leads. Its source code is available for study and modification. The bus still needs adaptation to local roads and testing. Bus manufacturer MAN is responsible for vehicle-control mechanisms and low-level software; the university handles sensor configuration and the driving system. After tests in controlled conditions, the partners plan operation on existing routes with personnel aboard to ensure safety.

The effort uses a joint research center established in October. It draws on experience deploying the Autoware automated-driving software in Japanese buses, but does not simply install unchanged software on another vehicle: both the vehicle platform and road conditions differ. A university professor describes federal support of 20 million euros over three years for the Munich bus-development project. That is project-wide funding, not an announced budget solely for Autoware software. The release supplies no Munich route-trial results, measured reduction in crashes or promise to remove the onboard safety personnel at the outset.

Automated driving cannot be transferred like a file that works identically on every vehicle. A computer needs sensor information and a way to change motion through the bus's mechanisms. The project therefore separates vehicle work from software work. Local roads add another set of conditions to check before an ordinary route can become the operating environment.

Passenger-route work is a planned stage in the announcement, not a published result. An onboard safety worker is part of that plan too. Automated does not mean people can already stop monitoring the journey, or that the road evaluation has been completed and the bus is ready for unrestricted service.

technology_signal.title: GXO and ASUS: separating robot plans from results
technology_signal.summary: Logistics company GXO plans to expand humanoid use after warehouse trials. ASUS is teaching a two-arm robot to pack computer accessories, but its stated speed and success rate remain targets.
technology_signal.implications: For GXO, up to a thousand warehouse robots is a conditional expansion plan. For ASUS, 99.5% success within 20 seconds is a kit-packing requirement rather than a published achieved result. The numbers describe different things and cannot be treated as equivalent measures of readiness.
